newsitem.title: INDIA: Namibia calls for revival of Non-Aligned Movement.
newsitem.headline: Namibia calls for revival of Non-Aligned Movement.

text.p: Namibian President Sam Nujoma started his visit to India on Friday with a call to revive the Non-Aligned Movement of developing countries that lost momentum after the collapse of the Soviet Union.
"We want to revive the Non-Aligned Movement in a much more meaningful manner," Nujoma told reporters at New Delhi's presidential palace after a ceremonial reception by President Shankar Dayal Sharma.
Nujoma, who is on a four-day visit, also urged Indian investors to promote cooperation between developing countries by investing in his mineral-rich nation.
The Non-Aligned Movement was originally organised to promote solidarity among newly independent nations and non-alignment to any superpower.
The 112-nation group has been criticised as having outlived its usefulness after the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.

But its leading members, including India, say the group retains its significance as a symbol of developing countries' solidarity in staying clear of superpower politics and pursuing economic progress.
With the end of the Cold War, the movement focuses mainly on political and economic divisions between the industrialised and developing worlds.
"The movement of the non-aligned countries has been a vehicle to promote the cause of the liberation of the oppressed people all over the world, and in Namibia in particular," said Nujoma.
"We have come here to specifically invite Indian businessmen and women to invest in Namibia and to enter into joint ventures with their counterparts in Namibia," he said.
Namibia became independent in 1990 after the withdrawal of troops sent by the then apartheid rulers of South Africa.
South Africa had said its troops were sent to counter the presence of Cuban troops in Angola.
Cuba's presence in the Non-Aligned Movement was a cause for criticism in Western nations, which saw Havana as an Eastern bloc ally.
Nujoma was scheduled to meet visiting Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral.
Hasina and Nujoma are due to speak on Saturday in New Delhi at an international conference of lawmakers seeking increased representation for women in parliaments around the world.
